notes: This file summarizes all confirmed, proposed, and failed Georgia 2026 statewide ballot measures as of March 7, 2026. The 2026 Georgia General Assembly session ends on Sine Die, April 2, 2026; additional measures could theoretically still be referred from bills that crossed over on March 6. However, constitutional amendments must pass both chambers with a two-thirds supermajority (120 House votes / 38 Senate votes) and cannot be initiated by citizens. No new constitutional amendments are expected after Crossover Day per normal legislative procedure.

confirmedBallotMeasures.officialTitle: Georgia Increase Acre Limit for Agriculture and Timber Conservation Use Property Tax Classification Amendment (2026)
confirmedBallotMeasures.ballotQuestion: Shall the Constitution of Georgia, for the purpose of protecting family farmland, be amended so as to increase the maximum acreage to qualify for assessment and taxation as a bona fide conservation use property from 2,000 acres to 4,000 acres?

mechanism.summary: Amends Article VII, Section I, Paragraph III(e)(1) of the Georgia Constitution to raise the acreage cap of 'bona fide conservation use property' that a single owner can enroll from 2,000 acres to 4,000 acres. Land enrolled in conservation use receives a reduced property tax assessment in exchange for a covenant to maintain the land in agricultural or timber use.
mechanism.effectiveDate: January 1, 2027 (if ratified by voters in November 2026)
mechanism.fiscalImpact: Reduces property tax revenue for local governments on newly eligible acreage above the 2,000-acre threshold; specific dollar amount not publicly estimated in available sources

confirmedBallotMeasures.yesVoteMeans: Increase the maximum acreage a single landowner can enroll in the conservation use property tax program from 2,000 to 4,000 acres, lowering their property tax burden in exchange for a land-use covenant.
confirmedBallotMeasures.noVoteMeans: Status quo; the 2,000-acre per-owner cap on conservation use enrollment remains in place.

presumed support — consistent with timber interests
largely supportive — 69 of 74 House Democrats voted yes

policyContext.background: Georgia's Conservation Use Value Assessment (CUVA) program allows qualifying agricultural and timber landowners to enroll acreage in exchange for a covenant to maintain conservation use; in return they pay taxes on a lower appraised value. The current cap of 2,000 acres per owner was set previously. Proponents argue family farm operations and timber tracts frequently exceed 2,000 acres and the cap limits the program's reach. Critics note the change primarily benefits larger landowners rather than small family farms.
policyContext.mainDebate: Whether raising the cap from 2,000 to 4,000 acres serves genuine family farm protection or primarily benefits large agricultural landowners and timber corporations with pass-through structures.

proposedMeasuresFailedOrDead.officialTitle: State Assurance of Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Amendment
proposedMeasuresFailedOrDead.sponsoredBy: Georgia Senate Republicans; co-authored by Sen. Greg Dolezal

mechanism.summary: Would have amended the Georgia Constitution in two ways: (1) changed 'Every person who is a citizen' to 'Only individuals who are citizens' in the voter eligibility clause — a clarifying change proponents argued strengthened the noncitizen voting prohibition; (2) constitutionally enshrined Georgia's existing photo ID requirement for voting, which is already required by state statute but not embedded in the state constitution.

proposedMeasuresFailedOrDead.officialTitle: Homestead Property Tax Phaseout Constitutional Amendment (proposed)
proposedMeasuresFailedOrDead.sponsoredBy: House Republican leadership; Speaker Jon Burns

mechanism.summary: Would have amended the Georgia Constitution to progressively reduce the assessed value of homestead property from the current 40% of market value down to 10% of market value by 2032–2037 (a reduction of 3 percentage points per year). This would effectively cut residential property tax bills for homeowners by up to 75%, phasing in over roughly a decade.
mechanism.fiscalImpact: Estimated to cost local governments and school districts billions of dollars in annual revenue; opponents argued it would devastate school funding that is heavily dependent on property taxes

failureDetails.houseVote: Approximately 99 yes, 73 no — needed 120 yes votes for two-thirds majority

The bill required all 99 House Republicans plus 21 Democrats — an effectively impossible coalition
Local governments and school boards opposed the measure due to revenue loss

proposedMeasuresFailedOrDead.aftermath: After HR 1114 failed, House Majority Leader Efstration said Republicans would pursue a statutory property tax cap instead (requiring only a simple majority). A bill to cap annual property tax increases at 3% reportedly did pass before Crossover Day.

policyContext.background: Georgia property taxes fund approximately 50-60% of K-12 school budgets and significant local government operations. Republican proponents argued homeowners face unaffordable tax increases tied to rising property values. Opponents (including the Georgia Budget and Policy Institute and local school superintendents) warned of catastrophic effects on public education funding.

proposedMeasuresFailedOrDead.officialTitle: Georgia Timber Sales Tax Exemption Constitutional Amendment (proposed)
proposedMeasuresFailedOrDead.shortName: Timber Harvest Ad Valorem Tax Exemption
proposedMeasuresFailedOrDead.proposedBallotDate: November 3, 2026 (if passed both chambers with two-thirds majority before April 2, 2026)

mechanism.summary: Would amend the Georgia Constitution to exempt standing timber from ad valorem (property) taxation at the point of harvest or sale, specifically for timber on land enrolled in a forest land conservation use covenant. The state would reimburse local governments for a portion of lost ad valorem revenue.
mechanism.fiscalImpact: Reduces local government property tax revenue; the state reimbursement mechanism is meant to offset local fiscal impact, but the net cost to state budget would increase

policyContext.background: Timber is Georgia's largest agricultural commodity. The industry faced severe economic hardship following Hurricane Helene (2024) and multiple sawmill closures. Proponents argue the ad valorem tax on standing timber penalizes landowners for holding timber until market conditions improve, discouraging conservation practices. The measure is companion to the already-passed HR 32 (conservation use acreage increase).
policyContext.industryContext: Georgia timber industry groups have lobbied aggressively following Hurricane Helene damage and mill closures

legislativeProcessNotes.howGeorgiaBallotMeasuresWork: Georgia does not allow citizen-initiated ballot measures (no initiative or referendum by petition at the state level). All statewide constitutional amendments must be referred by the Georgia General Assembly with a two-thirds supermajority vote (120 of 180 House members; 38 of 56 Senate members) during a single legislative session. The Governor's signature is NOT required for a constitutional amendment to go to the ballot. Amendments require simple majority (50%+1) voter approval to be ratified.
legislativeProcessNotes.postCrossoverProspects: Constitutional amendments must originate in one chamber and cross to the other before Crossover Day. Bills that have already crossed (e.g., Senate bills now in the House, or House bills now in the Senate) can still be amended and passed before Sine Die on April 2, 2026. However, no new constitutional amendment bills introduced after Crossover Day can advance in the same session. As of March 7, 2026, no additional constitutional amendments beyond HR 32 appear on track for the 2026 ballot.

evidenceSummary.overallConfidence: HIGH for statewide picture. The 2025 session produced exactly one constitutional amendment (HR 32) that was certified for the 2026 ballot. The 2026 session, which ends April 2, has so far produced no new constitutional amendments following Crossover Day failures of HR 450 (sports betting), SR 838 (voter ID), and HR 1114 (property tax elimination). HR 1000 (timber tax) remains technically possible before Sine Die but no passage evidence found.
